strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful extension of sparse MoE models: selected experts can be executed at variable nested widths, adding an orthogonal compute-control axis beyond top-k expert selection.
The method is simple and compatible with standard MoE FFN experts: width control is implemented by slicing the intermediate dimension, and the training recipe is easy to understand.

The experimental section covers several model sizes, routing settings, token budgets, and inference modes, and the Pareto-frontier plots consistently suggest that learned router-conditioned width allocation can improve perplexity/FLOP trade-offs.
The paper includes relevant ablations comparing uniform widths, probability-normalized widths, and learned test-time width allocation, supporting the claim that the learned gamma mapping matters.
The limitations section honestly notes that experiments are restricted to small-scale LMs trained from scratch.
weaknesses: A major soundness issue is training-compute fairness. MoSE pretraining runs both full width and a sampled width per minibatch, which appears to require roughly two forward/backward passes, while the MoE baseline is trained under the same token budget but not the same training compute. The full-width MoSE improvements over MoE may therefore partly reflect extra optimization compute or regularization rather than the architecture alone.

The inference comparisons are incomplete. The baseline MoE is mostly a fixed point, while MoSE gets many budgeted operating points plus test-time calibration. Stronger baselines such as varying top-k, router-threshold routing, elastic MoE variants, or calibration/adaptation of MoE routing are not evaluated head-to-head.

The central efficiency claim is based on theoretical MFLOPs per token, with no latency, throughput, memory bandwidth, batching, or hardware-kernel measurements. Since slicing expert FFNs and sparse routing can have nontrivial overhead, the claimed deployment benefits are not fully established.

The test-time training protocol is under-specified and potentially leaks distributional advantage: gamma is calibrated on OpenWebText and evaluated heavily on OpenWebText, with unclear held-out separation and no analysis of sensitivity to calibration data, batch count, optimizer, or budget selection.

Results lack uncertainty estimates, seeds, or significance analysis. Some reported downstream gains, especially on WSC with only 273 validation examples and LAMBADA accuracy fluctuations, may be within noise.

The scale is modest for the claims about LLMs and MoE scaling: the largest model is around 1B parameters and trained on up to 15B tokens, so extrapolation to modern large MoE systems remains speculative.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendix provides useful hyperparameters, but the paper does not provide code, seeds, exact data splits, full numeric Pareto tables, or detailed FLOP-counting formulas.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the main idea is a natural combination of slimmable networks and MoE experts, with a simple scalar test-time allocation rule. It is promising, but the conceptual novelty is incremental.

strengths: The paper targets a real limitation of sparse MoE models: expert selection is discrete, while the internal compute used by selected experts is usually fixed. The proposed nested slicing of expert FFNs is simple and plausible, and it gives a clear mechanism for producing multiple inference-time width/compute operating points from one checkpoint.

The experiments cover several small GPT-style model sizes, routing settings, token budgets, and inference policies. The paper also includes useful ablations comparing uniform width, fixed router-probability allocation, and learned test-time sharpness parameters.

The limitations section honestly acknowledges an important scope limitation: all results are on relatively small LLMs trained from scratch, so it is unclear whether the approach transfers to post-training or truly large-scale MoE systems.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not convincingly supported. MoSE training evaluates two widths per batch, which appears to require roughly two forward/backward passes, but the comparison to MoE is presented mainly at equal token count rather than equal training compute, wall-clock, or energy. This is a major confound: improved full-width performance may come from extra training computation or regularization rather than the proposed architecture.

The compute-budget formulation is technically underspecified and potentially inconsistent. Widths are assigned by proportional allocation and then clipped to [w_min,w_max], but there is no renormalization to enforce the stated budget. This means the actual compute can differ substantially from Gamma, especially for peaked router distributions, weakening claims about fixed-budget optimization and Pareto dominance.

The strongest results rely on test-time training of gamma using OpenWebText calibration batches, but the protocol is not sufficiently controlled. The paper does not clearly separate calibration, validation, and test data, does not report sensitivity to calibration set choice or size beyond one setting, and compares against limited baselines. A fair comparison should include similarly tuned uniform-width budgets and other adaptive allocation heuristics under identical calibration access.

The evidence is mostly FLOPs-based, with no measured latency, throughput, memory bandwidth, batching behavior, or kernel-efficiency analysis. Since slicing experts can create irregular small matrix operations and routing overheads, FLOP reductions alone may not translate into practical inference gains.

The experimental scale is modest relative to the claims about LLM and MoE deployment. GPT2-Small/Standard/Medium trained on OpenWebText are useful prototypes, but they do not establish behavior for modern large MoE systems, production routing, or pretrained dense-to-MoE/post-training workflows.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives some hyperparameters, but there are no seeds, variance/error bars, implementation details for routing capacity and token dropping, tokenizer/evaluation harness details, exact calibration/test splits, or released code. Many figures show Pareto curves without tabulated numerical values, making independent verification difficult.

Presentation overstates the results. Phrases such as consistently dominates Pareto frontiers and requiring no changes to the standard MoE pipeline are stronger than the evidence supports, especially given doubled training passes, calibration-time optimization, and the lack of training-compute-matched baselines.

The ethics/impact statement is perfunctory. Efficiency work on LLMs has deployment, access, and environmental implications, but the paper simply states that no societal consequences need highlighting, which is not an adequate treatment for an ICML submission.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful extension of MoE models: selected experts need not be executed at full width, and nested slimmable expert FFNs provide a simple mechanism for finer-grained accuracy-compute tradeoffs.

The method is technically straightforward and well motivated. The formulation cleanly separates expert selection from expert capacity, and the training recipe of full-width plus sampled-width losses is easy to integrate into standard MoE pretraining.

The empirical results are consistently positive across several axes: GPT2-Small/Standard/Medium scales, E8A2/E8A4/E16A4 routing settings, 3B-15B token budgets, uniform-width versus router-conditioned allocation, and downstream zero-shot evaluations on LAMBADA and WSC.

The ablations are helpful. In particular, the comparison against uniform width and normalized router-probability allocation supports the claim that learned test-time sharpness improves width assignment beyond a trivial probability heuristic.

The paper includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including architecture sizes, routing settings, token budgets, optimizer settings, width grid, calibration batch count, and FLOP breakdowns. The limitations section honestly notes that the study is restricted to small LLMs trained from scratch.
weaknesses: The main limitation is scale and external validity. The largest experiment is a 1B GPT-style model trained on OpenWebText, while the paper motivates deployment for modern large MoE LLMs. It remains unclear whether the same training stability, routing behavior, and savings hold at contemporary MoE scale.

The efficiency evidence is based on MFLOPs per token rather than actual latency, throughput, memory bandwidth, or hardware utilization. Slimming FFN hidden dimensions may not translate cleanly into wall-clock gains without specialized kernels, especially with per-token or per-expert dynamic widths.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates. There are no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance analyses, despite some gains being modest and downstream benchmarks such as WSC being small and noisy.

The baselines are somewhat narrow. The paper compares mainly to standard MoE, uniform MoSE, and simple router-probability allocation, but does not thoroughly compare against adaptive top-k routing, separately trained smaller-width MoEs, pruning/distillation baselines, or elastic MoE alternatives under matched training and inference budgets.

The test-time training setup needs sharper protocol detail. The calibration stream is drawn from OpenWebText, but the relationship between calibration data, validation/test data, and reported OpenWebText perplexities is not fully clarified; this matters because TTT directly optimizes language modeling loss under the target budget.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete: the paper gives many hyperparameters, but does not specify random seeds, exact tokenizer/data preprocessing, evaluation harness details, code availability, or enough operational detail to reproduce the reported FLOP accounting and dynamic-width inference behavior.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The paper acknowledges small-scale training, but does not discuss energy costs of training multiple MoE/MoSE models, deployment fairness/accessibility implications, or possible misuse considerations for more efficient language models.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically motivated extension of sparse MoE models: selected experts can be executed at variable nested widths, giving a finer-grained compute-quality tradeoff than changing only the number of active experts.

The method is technically simple and compatible with standard MoE training: width slicing of FFN hidden dimensions, two-width training, standard load-balancing/z-loss regularization, and a low-dimensional inference-time width policy based on router probabilities.

The empirical section is broad. The paper reports results across GPT-style scales, routing settings, training-token budgets, larger/finer-grained expert configurations, zero-shot tasks, and continual-pretraining adaptation of a DeepSeek-V2-Lite checkpoint.

The main results consistently show improved perplexity/FLOP Pareto frontiers over uniform-width MoSE and vanilla MoE baselines, and the paper includes useful diagnostics for runtime/FLOPs correlation and routing stability.
Presentation is generally clear, with equations and figures that make the architecture and inference policies easy to understand.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are mostly against vanilla MoE and uniform-width variants. The paper discusses elastic MoE and slimmable/nested model literature, but does not provide direct empirical comparisons to the closest adaptive-compute or elastic MoE alternatives, making the claimed significance harder to calibrate.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, multiple seeds, or statistical tests. Several downstream improvements are small, especially on WSC/SIQA, so it is unclear which gains are robust versus run or evaluation noise.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank; the appendices provide useful hyperparameters, but important implementation details for exact FLOP accounting, routing capacity behavior, calibration selection, and DeepSeek CPT adaptation are not enough to independently reproduce the full study.

The test-time training procedure uses OpenWebText calibration and is often evaluated on OpenWebText-like perplexity frontiers, which risks calibration/evaluation coupling. Transfer is shown for LAMBADA and a few tasks, but broader domain shift and budget-selection behavior remain underexplored.

The paper mainly reports MFLOPs/token; wall-clock measurements are limited to smaller diagnostic settings. For MoE systems, realized speedups can depend heavily on batching, kernels, memory access, expert parallelism, and hardware utilization, so the deployment claim is not fully established.

No meaningful limitations or ethics discussion is provided, despite training and adapting large language models. Compute cost, data provenance, possible downstream misuse, and deployment tradeoffs should be addressed.

Originality is moderate rather than high: combining slimmable/nested networks with MoE experts is a natural and elegant idea, but the conceptual ingredients are largely inherited from prior slimmable networks, nested representations, and MoE routing.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant efficiency problem in MoE language models: standard sparse routing selects experts, but each selected expert is still executed at full width, leaving a potentially useful axis of conditional computation unused.

The proposed MoSE architecture is conceptually simple and compatible with standard MoE FFN structure: experts are made nested/slimmable by slicing the intermediate hidden dimension, and the full-width model reduces to an ordinary MoE.

The manuscript includes a reasonably broad empirical sweep for an academic paper, covering GPT-style models from small to 2.5B, several expert/routing settings, zero-shot benchmarks, runtime diagnostics, and a continual-pretraining adaptation experiment on DeepSeek-V2-Lite.

The inference-time width allocation idea is practical: using router probabilities and learning only a shared or layer-wise sharpness parameter is lightweight, and the reported Pareto curves suggest meaningful potential FLOP reductions at matched perplexity.
weaknesses: The central empirical comparison is not fully convincing because MoSE training uses both full-width and sampled-width forward/backward passes per step, while the MoE baseline appears to receive the same token budget but not the same training compute. This makes claims that MoSE matches or improves full-width MoE capacity hard to attribute to the architecture rather than additional optimization cost or regularization.

The paper lacks strong baselines for adaptive inference. Comparisons are mainly against standard MoE, uniform widths, and a fixed normalized-probability rule; it does not adequately compare with existing elastic/slimmable transformer methods, structured pruning, early-exit/adaptive-compute methods, or continual-learning/post-training compression baselines under matched training and calibration budgets.

Several results are presented only as Pareto plots without enough numerical detail, uncertainty estimates, or repeated runs. There are no confidence intervals or seed analyses, despite small downstream benchmarks such as WSC and relatively modest accuracy differences in some tables.

The test-time training protocol raises evaluation concerns. Gamma is calibrated on OpenWebText and many main results evaluate OpenWebText perplexity or closely related language-modeling objectives; the paper does not clearly separate calibration, validation, and test data or quantify sensitivity to calibration distribution, size, and budget.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although the appendix gives some hyperparameters, many implementation details are missing or underspecified, including exact data preprocessing, evaluation prompts/templates, FLOP accounting conventions, checkpoint selection, calibration splits, and detailed DeepSeek continual-pretraining setup. The code link in the abstract appears blank.

The significance is reduced by overclaiming. The method is a natural combination of MoE routing and slimmable/nested networks, and the paper does not clearly establish why its particular slicing and scalar-gamma allocation strategy is technically novel beyond this combination.

The discussion of limitations and ethics is thin. The paper notes absence of frontier-scale from-scratch training, but does not sufficiently address hardware efficiency caveats, possible memory/latency bottlenecks from irregular widths, robustness across widths, or safety implications of adaptive model capacity.

Overall, the idea is promising and the paper contains useful preliminary evidence, but the evaluation and reproducibility weaknesses prevent others from reliably assessing or building on the claimed compute-quality improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely efficiency problem in MoE language models: standard sparse routing decides which experts to run but still executes selected experts at full width. Introducing nested slimmable expert FFNs is a simple, well-motivated extension that adds a useful second axis of conditional computation.

The method is technically straightforward and sound: expert widths are implemented by slicing the FFN hidden dimension, training uses full-width plus sampled-width losses with standard MoE auxiliary losses, and inference policies range from uniform widths to router-conditioned and test-time-trained width allocation.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this type of systems/modeling paper. Results cover multiple GPT-style model sizes, routing settings, token budgets, finer-grained expert regimes, zero-shot benchmarks, a 2.5B/50B-token setting, and continual-pretraining adaptation of DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Across these settings, the reported Pareto-frontier improvements and FLOPs reductions are consistent.

The ablations are helpful: uniform-width, normalized-probability, shared-gamma TTT, and layer-wise TTT are compared, supporting the claim that router probabilities are useful but that learning the probability-to-width mapping gives additional gains.

The paper includes useful diagnostics beyond headline perplexity, including training stability, width-wise convergence, routing stability, learned gamma behavior, FLOPs breakdown, and some latency/throughput measurements. These strengthen the evidence that the proposed training recipe is not simply destabilizing or collapsing routing.

Presentation is generally clear. The core mechanism is easy to understand, the figures communicate the compute-quality trade-offs effectively, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges that frontier-scale from-scratch MoE training is not demonstrated.
weaknesses: Originality is good but not transformative: the main idea is a natural combination of slimmable/nested networks with MoE experts, plus a low-dimensional router-probability-to-width calibration. The paper would be stronger with a sharper comparison to prior elastic-width transformer methods and elastic MoE methods beyond narrative related work.

The strongest claims rely heavily on FLOPs/token. The appendix includes runtime diagnostics, but only for limited settings; it is not fully established that the reported 30-40% FLOPs reductions translate to comparable latency or throughput gains in large production MoE inference, where kernels, batching, memory bandwidth, and irregular widths may dominate.

The evaluation lacks statistical uncertainty. Several table improvements are modest, especially for small zero-shot benchmarks such as WSC, and no seed variance or confidence intervals are reported. This makes it hard to distinguish robust gains from noise in some downstream results.

The test-time training setup needs clearer separation from evaluation. Gamma is calibrated on OpenWebText and OpenWebText perplexity is a central reported metric; although this is lightweight and low-dimensional, the paper should clarify calibration/evaluation splits and possible overfitting or selection effects across budgets.

Baseline coverage is somewhat narrow. The paper compares against vanilla MoE and internal MoSE inference variants, but does not experimentally compare with other elastic inference alternatives such as Elastic MoE/RoE-style approaches, dynamic top-k routing, expert dropping, or nested transformer/slimmable transformer baselines under matched training and inference budgets.

Reproducibility is incomplete as written: the abstract says code can be found at a blank location, and while hyperparameters and model configurations are provided, details such as exact data preprocessing, evaluation harness, random seeds, checkpoint selection, and implementation of FLOP counting/calibration are not sufficient for easy independent reproduction.

The limitations and ethics discussion are adequate but brief. The impact statement notes that behavior may vary across widths, but there is no empirical robustness, safety, bias, or calibration analysis across width regimes, which matters because the method explicitly changes model behavior as compute changes.
